method: Claude built a new generator family, best_play (folder acorn-game, shown as Acorn Game), for game trees and optimal play, a concept that two analysed tasks use (Seashells and Pebbles, Pirate Hunters) but no family covered. It keeps their idea (a side wins only with a move that works against every reply) under original games: a forked trail where the student chooses at yellow forks and a raccoon chooses at grey ones, and a take-away pile game against the same raccoon. The opponent is a story character that always plays its best, so the puzzle stays single-player. Levels 1-2 are trails (pick the first path; type how many acorns you can be sure of, three forks deep); levels 3-5 are piles (type the winning first move; pick the full list of lose-piles; a big pile where the moves allowed have gaps or the last acorn loses). Every problem passes check_best_play.py, which rebuilds the game from the picture and solves trails bottom-up and piles top-down (the generator does the reverse), and every corrupted answer key, tag, scene, picture and explanation ending in the mutation trials is caught. While building the checker Claude found that the generator had left the off-by-one habit untagged when the pile is already a multiple of the biggest move; a student with that habit takes the biggest move there, and the generator now tags it.

ladder.question: path
ladder.note: Pick the first path on a trail where the raccoon chooses next. The path with the biggest basket is a trap.

ladder.question: sure
ladder.note: Three forks deep (you, the raccoon, you): type how many acorns you can be sure of.

ladder.question: first
ladder.note: A small pile: type how many acorns to take first so you are sure to win.

ladder.question: traps
ladder.note: Find every lose-pile from 1 up: the pattern repeats.

ladder.question: first

generator_candidates.why: Game trees had no family. Random small trails (max and min forks) and take-away piles with varied move sets and endings; the winning move is unique and checked by full search; distractors from heading for the biggest prize, grabbing the most, and the wrong repeating pattern.

misconceptions.description: Heads for the biggest basket on the trail, forgetting that the raccoon chooses at its forks and will not let you reach it.
misconceptions.remediation: Play the raccoon's side yourself: at each grey fork, which way would you send your opponent?

misconceptions.description: Picks the path with the most acorns in all its baskets, as if the raccoon chose at random instead of choosing its best.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which single basket the raccoon would leave you on each path. The others do not count.

misconceptions.description: Chooses the first way toward the biggest basket, then plays well from there, without checking what the raccoon does on that side.
misconceptions.remediation: Work back from the baskets, fork by fork, before choosing the first way.

misconceptions.description: Lets the raccoon choose at every fork after the first, even at forks where it is your turn to choose.
misconceptions.remediation: Mark each fork with whose turn it is before working out any values.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up whose fork is whose, taking the smaller basket at your own forks and the bigger at the raccoon's.
misconceptions.remediation: Colour the forks: at yours take the most, at the raccoon's expect the least.

misconceptions.description: Takes as many acorns as allowed, as if getting the pile smaller fast were the goal.
misconceptions.remediation: After your move, ask what the raccoon can do. Can it reach a pile that is bad for you?

misconceptions.description: Thinks the lose-piles come every (biggest move) acorns, instead of every (biggest move + 1).
misconceptions.remediation: Check the smallest case: with the biggest move 3, can the player to move win from a pile of 3?

misconceptions.description: Uses the pattern for the other ending: plays as if the last acorn wins when it loses, or the other way round.
misconceptions.remediation: Reread the sign, then work out piles 1 and 2 by hand before using any pattern.

misconceptions.description: Uses the 'every biggest move + 1' pattern even though some move sizes are missing from the sign, which breaks that pattern.
misconceptions.remediation: Build the win and lose list from pile 1 upward with only the moves on the sign.

misconceptions.description: Guesses that even piles are the lose-piles, as if each player could take only one acorn.
misconceptions.remediation: Try pile 2 by hand: can the player to move take both acorns?

misconceptions.description: Finds the first lose-pile but does not see that the pattern repeats further up.
misconceptions.remediation: After the first lose-pile, keep going: which pile is next where every move leaves a win-pile?
